ai.definition: Neuromorphic hardware is a type of computer hardware designed to mimic the structure and function of biological neural networks, enabling more efficient processing of complex data.
ai.howItWorks: By using analog circuits to simulate neurons and synapses, neuromorphic hardware can process information in parallel, similar to how the human brain works. This allows for real-time processing and learning without the need for explicit programming, leading to energy-efficient and scalable solutions.
ai.problemSolved: Traditional digital computing systems are inefficient for tasks that require real-time processing of complex data, such as image recognition or natural language understanding. Neuromorphic hardware addresses this by providing a more biologically inspired approach that can handle these tasks with lower power consumption.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing neuromorphic hardware involves creating circuits that mimic the behavior of neurons and synapses using advanced semiconductor technologies. This includes designing and fabricating analog circuits on chips, which require precise control over materials and processes to achieve the desired performance characteristics.
ai.buildProcess: The build process for neuromorphic hardware typically starts with circuit design, followed by fabrication using specialized semiconductor processes. Testing and validation are crucial steps to ensure that the hardware operates as intended before integration into larger systems or devices.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the complexity of designing and fabricating analog circuits, the need for advanced manufacturing techniques, and the potential for high initial investment in research and development. As with any new technology, economies of scale could reduce costs over time if mass production becomes feasible.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook for neuromorphic hardware is promising as it addresses specific limitations of traditional computing systems. However, widespread adoption will depend on overcoming challenges related to standardization, integration with existing infrastructure, and the development of software tools that can effectively leverage its unique capabilities.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks are still evolving for neuromorphic hardware, but safety standards for electronic devices may apply. Specific regulations could emerge as this technology gains more widespread use in critical applications such as healthcare or autonomous vehicles.
ai.risks: Technical risks include the need for continued innovation to improve performance and reliability, as well as potential limitations in scalability and compatibility with existing systems. Business risks involve the high initial investment required for research and development, and the uncertainty around market demand and adoption rates.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain given the current stage of commercialization and limited applications. As more companies enter the field and successful use cases emerge, profitability could increase, but this will depend on factors such as cost reduction through manufacturing scale-up and the development of new markets.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development of neuromorphic hardware may focus on improving energy efficiency, expanding application areas beyond current niches like sensor networks, and developing more sophisticated learning algorithms that can operate in real-time environments. Advances in materials science could also play a role in enhancing performance and reducing costs.

glossary.def: Computer hardware designed to mimic the structure and function of biological neural networks, enabling efficient processing of complex data.
Electrical circuits that operate with continuous signals representing real-world values, as opposed to digital circuits which use discrete binary states.
The basic functional units of the nervous system, responsible for transmitting information through electrical and chemical signals.
The junctions between neurons where neurotransmitters are released to transmit signals from one neuron to another or to other cells such as muscle fibers.

subsystems.name: Neuron circuit
subsystems.role: emulates the integrate-and-fire behaviour of a biological neuron.

subsystems.name: Synapse array
subsystems.role: stores connection weights and delivers current to neurons.

subsystems.name: Interconnect fabric
subsystems.role: routes spikes between neurons as asynchronous events.

subsystems.name: Learning engine
subsystems.role: adjusts weights using local plasticity rules.

subsystems.name: I/O and sensors
subsystems.role: converts real-world signals into spikes and reads out results.

subsystems.name: Software toolchain
subsystems.role: maps spiking neural networks onto the hardware.

buildSteps.title: Design neuron and synapse cells
buildSteps.detail: Analog and mixed-signal circuit techniques are used to create membranes, thresholds and weight storage that behave like biological components.

buildSteps.title: Simulate the circuits
buildSteps.detail: Spice-level simulations verify spiking dynamics, timing and power consumption before committing to silicon.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the chip
buildSteps.detail: A CMOS process forms the core, with memristor or floating-gate elements added where non-volatile analog weights are needed.

buildSteps.title: Lay out the interconnect
buildSteps.detail: Asynchronous routing is arranged so spikes can travel between neurons without collisions or excessive delay.

buildSteps.title: Add on-chip learning
buildSteps.detail: Plasticity circuits are wired to synapses so weights can be updated locally based on spike timing.

buildSteps.title: Package and interface
buildSteps.detail: The die is packaged and connected to event-based sensors and standard digital I/O.

buildSteps.title: Develop the compiler
buildSteps.detail: Software maps trained spiking networks onto the physical neuron and synapse resources.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate and test
buildSteps.detail: Analog components are tuned to compensate for manufacturing variation, then the chip is tested on benchmark tasks.

prerequisites.why: neuron and synapse circuits rely on precise analog behaviour in standard silicon processes.
they can store synaptic weights in a tiny, non-volatile cell, but yield and variability remain challenges.
training methods that work well on conventional hardware do not always translate to spikes.
they produce the sparse, asynchronous data that neuromorphic hardware is designed to process.
event-based communication depends on efficient on-chip networks that can handle bursts of spikes.

pathway.milestone: Research chips such as Intel's Loihi, IBM's TrueNorth and SpiNNaker demonstrate spiking networks in the lab.
pathway.unlocks: understanding of how to build and program large spiking systems.

pathway.milestone: Chips with on-chip learning for always-on edge devices.
pathway.unlocks: ultra-low-power pattern recognition in sensors and wearables.

pathway.milestone: Integrated systems combining event-based sensors and neuromorphic processors.
pathway.unlocks: real-time, low-latency perception for robotics and autonomous systems.

pathway.milestone: Commercial neuromorphic processors that compete with conventional AI accelerators on efficiency.
pathway.unlocks: widespread use in battery-powered and embedded AI where power is the limiting factor.
